01.actor: Rabbi Ami and a man in his neighborhood
01.event: Rabbi Ami, after an investigation, publicly declared a neighbor to be a mamzer.
01.turn: The man went about weeping at the declaration.
01.outcome: Rabbi Ami consoled him that by making him publicly known he had given him life, since a known mamzer and his descendants survive.
01.summary: A man living near Rabbi Ami was investigated and declared a mamzer. He went about weeping. Rabbi Ami told him not to be upset, because by making his status known he had given him life.

02.actor: Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa, Nehunya the well digger and his daughter
02.event: Nehunya's daughter fell into the Great Cistern and Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa announced hour by hour that she was safe and then that she had come up.
02.turn: She said a ram led by an old man pulled her out; Rabbi Hanina explained he knew because God would not let the righteous man's own child come to harm from his public work.
02.outcome: She was saved. The passage itself adds only that Nehunya's son nonetheless died of thirst, illustrating that God is exacting with the righteous.
02.summary: The daughter of Nehunya the well digger fell into the Great Cistern. Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa reported hour by hour that she was at peace and then that she had come up. She said a ram led by an old man had pulled her out, and he explained he had been sure the righteous man's own child would not be harmed by his public work.
02.missing: The proposed passage [4] is only a later comment (Rabbi Abba) that Nehunya's son died of thirst, citing verses; the narrative itself is in the context segments, and the son's death is only mentioned, not narrated.

03.actor: An Amorite and an Israelite resident of Eretz Yisrael
03.event: The Amorite asked how much fruit the Israelite could pick from a palm tree by the Jordan and was told sixty kor.
03.turn: The Amorite taunted that Israel had ruined the land since his people picked 120 kor.
03.outcome: The Israelite retorted that he had only been speaking of one side of the tree.
03.summary: An Amorite asked a resident of Eretz Yisrael how much he could pick from a palm tree on the Jordan's bank. He said sixty kor, and the Amorite scoffed that they used to pick 120, so Israel had ruined the land. The resident answered that he had only counted one side of the tree.

04.event: Aher saw the tongue of Hutzpit the interpreter, who had been executed, being dragged along the street by a pig.
04.turn: He cried out, 'Shall a mouth that produced pearls lap dirt?'
04.outcome: He left the fold and sinned.
04.summary: According to one account, Aher saw the tongue of the executed Hutzpit the interpreter being dragged in the street by a pig. He asked how a mouth that produced pearls could lap up dirt. That sight led him to go out and sin.

05.actor: The people of the Upper Galilee and a poor man of noble descent from Tzippori
05.event: They bought him a litra of meat every day.
05.summary: The people of the Upper Galilee bought a litra of meat every day for a poor man of good family from Tzippori. Later sages ask why this was remarkable and suggest it was expensive poultry, a litra's weight in coins, or an animal slaughtered daily just for him.
05.missing: There is no turn or resolution, only a bare report of an act of charity followed by discussion of what made it remarkable.

06.actor: Rava and a Sage questioning him
06.event: In a good mood Rava boasted he was like ben Azzai ready to answer any question; a Sage asked how many apples make an eiruv and Rava replied that one does not make an eiruv with apples.
06.turn: The Sage objected from a mishna that all foods combine for the eiruv measure, showing apples do count.
06.outcome: Rava's boast was undercut: his dismissive answer was shown wrong by the mishna.
06.summary: Rava, feeling sharp, declared he was like ben Azzai and could answer anything. A Sage asked how many apples are needed for an eiruv, and Rava asked whether one even makes an eiruv with apples. The Sage answered with a mishna showing that all foods, apples included, count toward the measure.
06.missing: The explicit conclusion that Rava conceded is not stated; it comes through the follow-up discussion.

07.event: A noblewoman tried to seduce Rav Kahana, a seller of palm-leaf baskets.
07.turn: He said he would go adorn himself, climbed to the roof and threw himself off; Elijah came and caught him.
07.outcome: Elijah complained he had been made to travel four hundred parasangs, Kahana blamed poverty, and Elijah gave him a basket of dinars.
07.summary: Rav Kahana sold palm-leaf baskets and a noblewoman tried to seduce him. He said he would go adorn himself, went up on the roof and fell, and Elijah caught him, complaining of the long journey. Kahana said poverty had put him in this position, so Elijah gave him a basket of dinars.

08.actor: Reish Lakish, Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yohanan
08.event: A man testified before Reish Lakish that another was a priest because he read first in synagogue; Reish Lakish demanded evidence of receiving teruma at the threshing floor, and Rabbi Elazar objected that the priesthood does not lapse where there is no threshing floor.
08.turn: Later the same kind of case came before Rabbi Yohanan, who said exactly what Rabbi Elazar had said; Reish Lakish realized Elazar had been quoting Yohanan.
08.outcome: Reish Lakish glared at Rabbi Elazar and rebuked him for not citing the statement in Yohanan's name.
08.summary: A man came before Reish Lakish claiming another was a priest because he read first in synagogue. Reish Lakish asked whether he had seen him receive teruma at the threshing floor, and Rabbi Elazar replied that the priesthood does not cease where there is no threshing floor. Later Rabbi Yohanan said the same thing in a similar case, and Reish Lakish glared at Elazar for not having said it in Yohanan's name.

09.missing: Rav's statement about the sandal he would use for halitza is a halakhic remark with a passing reference to what he saw Rabbi Hiyya do; no event is told.

10.actor: Rav Sheshet and a man passing his father-in-law's house
10.event: Rav Sheshet had a man lashed for merely passing the entrance of his father-in-law's house.
10.turn: The Gemara explains the man was suspected of misconduct with his mother-in-law.
10.summary: A man who only passed by the entrance to his father-in-law's house was lashed by Rav Sheshet. It is explained that he was suspected with his mother-in-law, so even passing by lent credence to the rumor.
10.missing: The incident is a brief precedent inside a legal question; no detail of what happened beyond the lashing.

11.event: Rabbi Yirmeya went out to the villages, where he was asked whether an eiruv may be made with moist beans.
11.outcome: On returning to the study hall he was told Rabbi Yannai's ruling that one may, with a handful.
11.summary: Rabbi Yirmeya visited some villages and was asked whether moist beans can be used for an eiruv. He did not know. Back in the study hall he was told that Rabbi Yannai permits it.

12.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and his son
12.event: Rabbi arranged his son's marriage into Rabbi Hiyya's family but the bride died as the contract was being written, so they checked the families' ancestry; he then arranged a match with the family of Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra.
12.turn: The son, promised twelve years of study first, saw the bride and first shortened it to six years and then asked to marry first; he was ashamed before his father, who reassured him.
12.outcome: He married and then studied twelve years; on return his wife was infertile and, after he prayed, she was healed.
12.summary: Rabbi arranged his son's marriage into Rabbi Hiyya's family, but the bride died as the contract was being written, and they investigated the family lines. He then arranged another match, and the son, who had agreed to study twelve years first, saw the bride and asked to marry first, and was ashamed before his father. After his twelve years of study his wife was infertile until he prayed for her and she was healed.
12.missing: What disqualification the ancestry check revealed is only hinted at.

13.actor: A woman whose bill of divorce was closer to her, and her husband and brother-in-law
13.event: In a precedent, a bill of divorce was closer to the woman than the man and was then lost.
13.turn: After the husband died, the court did not rely on it.
13.outcome: They required her to perform halitza.
13.summary: Rav Mordekhai told Rav Ashi of a past case where a bill of divorce was closer to the woman and was lost. After her husband died, they still required her to perform halitza rather than rely on the divorce.
13.missing: Who the people were and what happened are not described; it is a bare precedent cited for a legal point.

14.missing: Rav Nachman's instruction to clear the earth is cited only as evidence for a legal position; nothing is narrated beyond that and the Gemara's reasoning.

15.event: Rabbi Tarfon used to bend down so his mother could climb onto and step down from her bed using him, and he boasted of this in the study hall.
15.turn: The Sages told him he had not reached even half of the honor due, asking whether she had ever thrown his purse into the sea in front of him without his shaming her.
15.outcome: His boast was met with a rebuke showing his honoring fell short; no reply is given.
15.summary: Rabbi Tarfon would bend down so his mother could climb into and out of bed on him, and he praised himself for this in the study hall. The Sages told him he had not reached half the honor due, asking whether he would have stayed calm had she thrown his purse into the sea.

16.event: A feather landed on Ameimar's head while he was judging, and a man removed it.
16.turn: The man said he had a case before him.
16.outcome: Ameimar said he was disqualified from judging the case; Mar Ukva did the same with a man who covered spittle in front of him.
16.summary: While Ameimar sat in judgment a feather landed on his head and a man removed it, then said he had a case before him. Ameimar said he was disqualified from judging it because of the favor. Mar Ukva did likewise with a man who covered spittle before him.

17.actor: The Sages examining a bill of divorce signed Anan bar Hiyya
17.event: A bill of divorce was found in Sura by an Anan bar Hiyya of Neharde'a, and the Sages searched all the way to Neharde'a and found only one other man of that name, from Hagra.
17.turn: Witnesses said that Anan bar Hiyya of Hagra was with them in Neharde'a on the day the get was written.
17.outcome: Abaye and Rava then each argue whether the doubt about identity matters; no conclusion on the case itself is told.
17.summary: A bill of divorce turned up in Sura signed by Anan bar Hiyya of Neharde'a. The Sages searched and found only one other man of that name, from Hagra, but witnesses said he was with them in Neharde'a that day. The rest is Abaye and Rava debating whether the doubt matters.
17.missing: No outcome for the woman is narrated; segments [5] and [6] are legal reasoning.

18.event: A reservoir in Yavne presumed to hold the required amount was measured and found deficient, and Rabbi Tarfon declared the immersions in it pure while Rabbi Akiva declared them impure.
18.turn: They argued by analogies to a priest on the altar found to be disqualified, and Akiva made his case by distinguishing the types of disqualification.
18.outcome: Rabbi Tarfon accepted Akiva's reasoning, saying that anyone who separates from him is separating from life.
18.summary: A reservoir in Yavne was measured and found short of the required amount. Rabbi Tarfon held the earlier immersions pure and Rabbi Akiva impure, and they argued by comparing it to a priest found disqualified at the altar. Akiva explained the difference between disqualifications and Tarfon accepted, telling him that to part from him is to part from life.
18.missing: It is mostly a legal debate, with the incident only as its starting point.

19.missing: Rabba bar Avuh's offer to give his daughter to Rav Nachman if his body steams is cited only to test a legal view of the signs of a eunuch; no event or outcome is narrated.

20.missing: A baraita about the origin of a permission for the Heker well: it states a rule with a note on the exiles encamping there and the prophets or custom permitting it, but there is no event, turn or ending.
